source.title: Chimera: Designing and Chinchilla-Scaling Hybrid Visual Diffusion Transformers
source.authors: Chong-Jian Ge; Hanwen Jiang; Tianyu Wang; Jiu-Xiang Gu; Yi-Ran Xu; Zi-Wen Chen; Shao-Teng Liu; Jing Shi; Yi-Cong Hong; Ze-Fan Cai; Hai Jin; Hao Tan

record.tranche_reason: The study fits scaling laws for visual diffusion and shows that changing the hyperparameter-transfer setup (HeteroP versus standard parameterization) shifts the estimated compute-optimal allocation. This refines the scope of scaling-law claims and directly bears on fit dependence.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own image- and video-diffusion scaling sweeps, compute-optimal frontiers, and comparisons of scaling estimates under HeteroP and standard parameterization. Cited language-model scaling results are not recorded as findings. Downstream benchmark scores and architecture-efficiency comparisons do not test the listed downstream-predictability or architecture-shape versions.
record.test_reason: The study fits its own Chinchilla-style scaling laws (loss surface, envelope, IsoFLOP) for image and video diffusion pretraining, a new setting. It also refits the image law under standard parameterization, which shows the fitted compute-optimal split depends on the training setup. It is a new-setting test (T3) with a V7 component rather than a T5 argument against a version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that with HeteroP-tuned models, all three Chinchilla estimators agree that image diffusion pretraining splits compute nearly evenly between activated parameters and visual tokens. Video modestly favours model size at higher budgets. Standard parameterization biases the fitted law toward oversized, undertrained models, so the authors call HeteroP a prerequisite for reliable compute-optimal laws.
record.recipe_differences: Adapts Chinchilla-style loss-surface and IsoFLOP methods to rectified-flow visual diffusion, activated parameters, visual latent tokens, image/video mixtures, and a hybrid architecture. Adds HeteroP module-wise hyperparameter transfer; it is not a language-model reproduction.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted compute-optimal exponents change substantially between HeteroP and standard parameterization. Image and video also yield different frontiers. Envelope, IsoFLOP, and parametric methods agree closely for images and on the direction of the video allocation, but video parametric-fit uncertainty is broad.

fits_no_version.finding: For image loss, the IsoFLOP-optimal image:video sample ratio falls from about 4:1 to 3:1 over 10¹⁸–10¹⁹ FLOPs (power-law exponent −0.08). For video loss, the optimum sits at the 1:1 boundary.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The compute-optimal data-mixture ratio between modalities follows a power law in compute.

record.problems: The paper reports a broad 80% bootstrap interval for the video exponent ([0.47, 0.80]) and says the video terminal checkpoints span only 0.7 decades in D. The scaling evidence comes from one visual-diffusion model family and uses activated parameters and the compute approximation C ≈ 6ND.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported scaling-law results were omitted.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining loss. The visual power-law loss fits are recorded under V5.

No test that small-run fits predict losses of runs orders of magnitude larger. The final 2.2B model was chosen from the frontier, but predicted vs observed loss is not reported. Only leave-one-model-out interpolation (R19) is given.
Language models and the Kaplan-versus-Hoffmann disagreement are not tested. Only the visual-diffusion allocation with activated parameters and C≈6ND is.
Width and depth vary, but never at fixed parameter count. The Fig. 7 sweeps only show larger models are better.
Repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are untested. All runs are under one epoch, in the infinite-data regime.
GenEval, DPG and FID are reported only for final models, not as a function of scale or loss.
Parameter counting (activated only), training schedule (constant LR only) and data distribution beyond the image/video split are not varied.

missing.what: Optimal image:video ratio vs compute: exponent −0.08 for image loss, boundary 1:1 for video loss, quadratic surface RMSE ≤2.4×10⁻³.
SP law prescribes a model about 1.2× larger per decade of compute, roughly 2× oversized when extrapolated three decades beyond the fitted range.
Fitted irreducible losses nearly identical across modalities (E=0.126 vs 0.124).

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T5 to T3: the core results apply the scaling-law framework in a new setting (visual diffusion) and mostly behave as the versions say. V3 and V7 are treated as applying in this new setting; V5 carries the modality extension. All runs use a constant LR schedule, activated-parameter counting, under one epoch, and a single architecture family. The SP comparison covers image only. Training loss is used as the metric, not a held-out loss.

versions.untested_parts: The study scales visual diffusion models, not language models, and does not test the stated language-model held-out pretraining-loss law.
It reports image leave-one-model-out validation and video held-out terminal-loss prediction, but does not test whether fits on small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
Tests visual diffusion using activated parameter count and visual latent positions under C ≈ 6ND; does not test the language-model-specific Kaplan-versus-Hoffmann comparison.
The study varies model width and depth for scaling and hyperparameter-transfer analyses, but does not isolate whether architecture details at a fixed parameter count change loss only slightly.
Tests image and video visual diffusion pretraining. Does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Reports downstream image-generation benchmarks and video metrics, but does not test whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or pretraining loss.

Tests sensitivity to HeteroP versus standard parameterization and compares three estimators. Does not systematically vary data, training schedule, parameter-count definitions, or fitting methods beyond those comparisons.
